name: Meta-Policy Reflexion: Reusable Reflective Memory and Rule Admissibility for Resource-Efficient LLM Agent
authors: Chunlong Wu, Ye Luo, Zhibo Qu, Min Wang (Tongji University)
feedback_source: self-generated (LLM hindsight reflection on failed trajectories); environment-reward (binary episode success/failure) triggers reflection; environment/user-defined constraint set used for hard admissibility checks
iteration_structure: episodic-retry-with-reset (multi-round trials over the same task set; memory updated after failed episodes, then frozen at inference)
reflection_object: Reflection operates on the failed action trajectory and is distilled into structured rules/constitution: episodic textual reflections are consolidated into predicate-like rules stored in an external Meta-Policy Memory (MPM). The base LLM remains a frozen policy generator; what is modified/grown is the external structured rule memory plus a prompt/context-level guidance layer, never model weights.
requires_training: none (no gradient/weight updates; LLM is frozen; 'training' refers only to memory-rule accumulation rounds)
reward_or_critic_model: self-as-judge (the same LLM acts as the reflection function f that analyzes failed trajectories and emits corrective rules); environment provides verifiable success/failure signal and a hard admissibility constraint set, but no trained reward or critic model is used
distillation_target: structured-rules/constitution: reflections are distilled into a compact, predicate-like Meta-Policy Memory (MPM) of generalized corrective rules with confidence weights (e.g., 'IF goal is to cool an object THEN place in fridge, NOT microwave'), forming a reusable cross-task rulebook/playbook.
emergent_vs_engineered: engineered (prompt/scaffold-engineered): MPR is an explicit hand-designed framework (reflection function, predicate memory, soft prompt injection, post-hoc admissibility filter); the reflective behavior is scaffolded, not RL-emergent.
memory_type: structured-notes/graph (Meta-Policy Memory: a structured, predicate-like, persistent rule store / playbook-cheatsheet of corrective rules with confidence weights)
memory_persistence: cross-task (rules accumulated over training rounds on a 60-task training set transfer to and are applied on a 74-task held-out test set; memory is frozen at inference)
memory_curation_mechanism: append-only consolidation with confidence weighting: failed trajectories are reflected upon and new predicate rules are unioned into memory (M <- M union f(tau)); rules carry confidence weights. The authors note rules may contain redundancies/inconsistencies and explicitly flag systematic verification, pruning, redundancy detection, and rule abstraction as future work (not yet implemented).
error_localization_granularity: step-level / action-level: reflection analyzes failure points in the action trajectory and extracts corrective rules tied to states/actions; hard admissibility validates each generated action against a per-state constraint set C(s_t).
intra_task_vs_inter_task: inter-task: the central contribution is transferring consolidated reflective knowledge across tasks (train on 60 tasks, evaluate on 74 held-out tasks without per-task reflection), contrasted with Reflexion's per-episode/per-task ephemeral traces.
failure_recovery_vs_avoidance: avoidance-only with in-step admissibility filtering: corrective rules avoid repeating mistakes in later episodes/tasks (retry across episodes); the hard admissibility check additionally blocks invalid/unsafe actions at generation time by resampling or falling back to a safe action, but there is no mid-trajectory reasoning recovery mechanism.
task_domains: embodied/decision-making (text-based interactive agent tasks); tool-use/action selection in a simulated household environment
headline_result: On ALFWorld with Qwen3-32b as the frozen base LLM, MPR trained 5 rounds on a 60-task training set and evaluated once on the 74-task held-out test set reaches 87.8% execution accuracy vs Reflexion's 86.9% (after 6 in-situ reflection rounds on the test set); adding hard admissibility checks (HAC) raises MPR to 91.4%.
baselines: Reflexion (verbal reinforcement learning); ReAct is referenced as a related per-episode baseline approach. Quantitative comparison is primarily MPR (and MPR+HAC) vs Reflexion.
gains_vs_baseline: Held-out 74-task test set: MPR 87.8% vs Reflexion 86.9% (+0.9 pts) with far fewer test-time reflection rounds (1 eval pass after 5 training rounds vs Reflexion's 6 in-situ rounds); MPR+HAC 91.4% vs Reflexion 86.9% (+4.5 pts). On the 60-task training set, MPR beats Reflexion every round: Round 1 83.9% vs 70.0% (+13.9 pts), Round 2 98.3% vs 84.4%, reaching 100% by Round 3 (vs Reflexion plateauing at 87.2-88.3% in Rounds 3-5).
compute_cost_profile: Positioned as resource-efficient / lightweight: no gradient steps, no weight updates, frozen off-the-shelf LLM, contrasted explicitly against RL approaches that require substantial parameter updates and compute. Memory guidance is purely prompt-level (no logit manipulation). Test-time efficiency claim: MPR generalizes with a single evaluation pass after 5 training rounds, vs Reflexion needing 6 in-situ reflection rounds on the test set; an exact per-call token/API multiplier is not quantified in the paper.
known_limitations: (1) Domain regularities: rapid convergence to 100% on training set suggests ALFWorld tasks share strong structural regularities that predicate rules capture; gains may not transfer to more heterogeneous domains and may need richer representations or longer adaptation. (2) Rule quality/interpretability: LLM-generated rules may contain redundancies or inconsistencies; no systematic verify/prune/compose mechanism yet. (3) Evaluation scope: single-agent, text-based only (one benchmark, ALFWorld); scaling to multimodal, multi-agent, or real-world API settings needs additional design for rule grounding and conflict resolution. Authors recommend per-task inspection to confirm genuine generalization vs dataset-specific coincidence.
oracle_or_external_feedback_dependency: env-reward plus external constraint-set: improvement signal comes from environment success/failure (which episodes failed) used to trigger reflection, and the hard admissibility check relies on an environment- or user-specified constraint set C(s). It does not require ground-truth answer labels for the reflection itself (reflection is self-generated), but it does depend on environmental task-completion feedback and externally specified admissibility constraints rather than being purely intrinsic.
self_correction_efficacy: net-positive (in the reported single-benchmark setting): MPR consistently improves execution accuracy over Reflexion on ALFWorld and HAC further raises robustness to 91.4%; however efficacy is plausibly task-dependent given the authors' caveat that ALFWorld's structural regularity may inflate gains, and evidence is limited to one benchmark.
calibration_effect: not-measured (the paper does not measure confidence calibration or a reasoning-tax/overconfidence effect; it reports execution accuracy and robustness only)
failure_attribution_capability: n/a (MPR is a memory/reflection method, not a failure-attribution method; it extracts corrective rules from failed trajectories but does not provide a failure-mode taxonomy or responsible-agent/step attribution framework)
failure_mode_addressed: Targets repeated failures across tasks that share latent structure, inefficient exploration / trial-and-error, limited cross-task adaptability, and superficial/ephemeral reflection (Reflexion-style traces discarded after use); HAC additionally targets invalid/unsafe actions (e.g., attempting to use objects not present in the environment). Relates to MAST-style modes such as superficial self-reflection and repeated/error-loop failures, though the paper does not map to MAST explicitly.
dataset_or_benchmark_released: No new reusable benchmark/dataset released; evaluation uses the existing ALFWorld benchmark. Per-trial breakdowns and raw logs are referenced as provided in an uploaded spreadsheet, but no formally released public artifact is confirmed.
builds_on: Reflexion (Shinn et al., 2023, verbal reinforcement learning); ReAct (Yao et al., 2022, reasoning+acting); ALFWorld (Shridhar et al., 2020) as the environment. Situated against memory works including A-Mem (arXiv:2502.12110), Memory-R1 (arXiv:2508.19828), G-Memory (arXiv:2506.07398), and the memory-mechanism survey (Zhang et al., arXiv:2404.13501).
reasoning_model_native: no / not-native: MPR treats the LLM as a frozen external policy generator and adds an external memory + admissibility layer; it does not target or rely on o1/R1-style built-in reflective reasoning models. Base model used is Qwen3-32b (a standard non-reasoning-specialized policy LLM in this setup).
on_policy_distillation_link: Weak/contrasting link: MPR distills reflective experience into an external symbolic rule memory rather than into model weights, explicitly avoiding on-policy distillation / RL-based parameter updates. It is positioned as the training-free, in-context alternative to on-policy distillation/skill-optimization-into-weights approaches.
sample_efficiency: High in the reported setting: MPR reaches 100% on the 60-task training set by Round 3 (vs Reflexion ~87% plateau), and generalizes to the 74-task held-out test set with only 5 training rounds + 1 evaluation pass (vs Reflexion needing 6 in-situ reflection rounds on the test set), indicating fewer reflection iterations to reach comparable-or-better accuracy.
